whyCorrect: Track what duplex working changes. Before it, the wire carried "one message at a time in one direction"; duplex cancels an operator's own signals at his own receiver so each end can send while the other sends. That takes the wire from one simultaneous message to two, and the blank names that result: the capacity was doubled, with no new copper needed.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text is being gauged or quantified; the sentence reports a change in what the wire can do, not an act of measurement.
whyWrong.B: "Protected" would suit shielding the line from damage or interference, but the point is an increase in throughput, not the preservation of something at risk.
whyWrong.D: "Restored" implies capacity had been lost and was brought back. The wire never had more capacity than one message; duplex adds capacity it never had.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a vague positive word instead of the specific quantity the passage's own logic supplies.
tips: When a blank follows a described mechanism, work out what the mechanism actually produces before you look at the choices.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank defines it: "small differences in spacing grow until vehicles arrive in pairs." A late bus picks up more passengers and falls further behind; the bus behind picks up fewer and gains. The gap feeds itself, so the pattern is self-reinforcing.

whyWrong.A: This is the exact opposite. A self-correcting pattern would shrink the gaps, but the text says the differences grow.
whyWrong.B: The bunching is plainly perceptible — buses arrive in pairs with a long gap behind them.
whyWrong.C: Nothing ties the effect to time of year; the cause given is passenger loading, which operates on any day.

tips: A colon after a blank is a definition — read past it before choosing.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets up a contrast with "rather than successive," so the blank must mean the opposite of one thing following the other. The singer cannot pause to search for a phrase, so he composes while performing, using ready-made word groups that fit the metre. Composition and performance happen at the same moment: they are simultaneous.

whyWrong.A: The singer is performing before an audience, so the activity is public, and "private" is not the opposite of "successive."
whyWrong.C: Rehearsal would mean the words were prepared in advance, which contradicts the point that the phrases are assembled on the spot.
whyWrong.D: The passage describes an oral tradition; writing is not in view, and "written" does not contrast with "successive."

commonMistakes: Ignoring the "rather than X" frame, which fixes the required meaning before you read the options.

whyCorrect: Substitute each meaning into the passage's own description. What the first encounter leaves behind is a population of cells that, on a second encounter, respond in days rather than weeks. "Memory" here names that stored capacity for a faster second response, which is what a vaccine sets up.

whyWrong.A: That is a memoir — a written account. The text describes cells, not a document.
whyWrong.B: This is the everyday psychological sense. No one is recalling anything; the immune system has no conscious faculty in play here.
whyWrong.D: Computer storage is a metaphorical extension. Nothing is being stored and read back as data; what persists is a population of responsive cells.

tips: For an underlined-word question, plug your candidate meaning back into the sentence and check it against the surrounding evidence, not against the word's most familiar sense.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts the single case with the aggregate: unpredictable singly, but ____ in the aggregate. The text already told you what the aggregate looks like — the proportion of ten thousand houses that burns "varies very little from one year to the next." A quantity that barely varies is regular.

whyWrong.A: The losses across ten thousand houses are the insurer's whole business; they are anything but invisible.
whyWrong.B: Fires are costly whether you look at one house or ten thousand, so "costly" draws no contrast with the single unpredictable case.
whyWrong.D: "Impossible" contradicts the passage, which says the aggregate proportion is steady and therefore workable.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word about the fires themselves rather than about their predictability, which is the property the sentence is comparing.

whyCorrect: The preceding sentence states a problem: a purified protein is safe but provokes little response because the immune system "finds nothing else amiss." The underlined sentence introduces adjuvants, which create the local disturbance that was missing and draw in the cells needed to spread the protein. It supplies the fix for the shortcoming just named.

whyWrong.B: It adds new information — a substance, its effect, and its mechanism — rather than saying the same thing again in different words.
whyWrong.C: The opposite: it explains how purified proteins are made to work, which is why they can be used.
whyWrong.D: No pathogen is named in the underlined sentence, and no vaccination failure is described anywhere in the text.

tips: Function questions turn on the relationship between sentences; read the one before the underline and ask what job the underline does for it.

whyCorrect: The text has two halves. First a claim — Parry argued from the Greek text that the recurring tags were the poet's tools. Then a test — he and Lord recorded living singers who worked without written texts, and those singers behaved exactly as the claim predicted. The purpose is to describe how a claim about an ancient text was checked against a living tradition.

whyWrong.A: No dating comparison is made. The Yugoslav singers are used as evidence about method, not about age.
whyWrong.B: Metre appears only as a detail — phrases fill a metrical position — and is never explained.
whyWrong.C: The recording equipment is mentioned in one clause as a means; it is not the subject of the passage.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that names something the text mentions rather than what the text is doing.

whyCorrect: Every detail points one way: the pollinators are bats, which navigate by echo; the leaf above each flower is dish-shaped and stiff so it returns a strong echo from many directions; and bats found a feeder in half the time when such a dish was added. The closing line names the idea — the plant advertises in the medium its pollinators use.

whyWrong.A: Nectar richness is never compared with that of other species; the text only says bats take almost all of it.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the passage. The stiff dish returns a stronger echo than an ordinary leaf.
whyWrong.D: No comparison between night and day appears anywhere in the text.

tips: A main-idea choice has to cover the experiment as well as the description; a detail that only fits one sentence is not the main idea.

whyCorrect: The text gives the trade directly: reheating "lets part of that strain relax," and the result is "a little softer than the quenched steel and far less liable to break." So the tool loses a small amount of hardness and gains toughness, which is why an edge tool is tempered rather than used straight from the quench.

whyWrong.A: The file appears only as a sign of how hard the quenched steel is not — it chips brittle steel. Reheating is not done so the tool can be filed.
whyWrong.B: Tempering makes the steel softer, not harder; the passage says so explicitly.
whyWrong.D: No shape change is described. What the sudden cooling produces is internal strain, not distortion that needs correcting.

commonMistakes: Assuming any heat treatment must improve hardness, when the text states tempering trades a little hardness for toughness.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that the second dose did more than put the level back where the first dose had it. The first dose's own peak in the table is 88 units at week 4. After the second dose the two-dose group reads 210 units at week 12 and is still at 140 at week 24 — both far above 88 — so the second dose pushed the level past the earlier peak rather than merely restoring it.

whyWrong.A: Week 4 is before the second dose was given, so this reading says nothing about what the second dose did; it only shows the two groups started alike.
whyWrong.B: This describes the decline of the single-dose group. It shows the first dose fading, not that the second dose exceeded the first dose's peak.
whyWrong.C: A fall from 210 to 140 is a decline within the two-dose group. It works against the conclusion rather than supporting it, and 140 still exceeds 88 only because of what happened earlier.

commonMistakes: Quoting the largest change in the table instead of the comparison the conclusion actually requires — post-boost level against the first dose's peak.

whyCorrect: The conclusion has two halves, and the evidence must cover both. "Slightly less often" is the mean headway rising from 8.0 to 8.4 minutes; "shortened passenger waits" is the mean wait falling from 6.2 to 4.7 minutes. Only this choice pairs those two rows, so only it shows waits falling in spite of the less frequent service.

whyWrong.A: One number from one rule. It gives no comparison at all, so it cannot support a claim about a change.
whyWrong.C: The drop in bunching describes the steadier spacing, but it leaves out both the wait time and the increased headway that the conclusion says was overcome.
whyWrong.D: A single standard deviation figure with nothing to compare it to; it does not mention waits.

tips: When a conclusion contains a concession ("even though …"), the right evidence has to include the conceded fact, not just the favourable one.

whyCorrect: "Redistributed rather than added" means sand moved from one part of the shore to another, so you need gains on one side set against losses on the other. North of the groyne the beach went 34 to 41 and 30 to 48; south of it, 31 to 19 and 33 to 26. Widening upstream of the drift and narrowing downstream is exactly the pattern of sand being trapped and withheld, not created.

whyWrong.B: That the immediately north station is widest in 2008 shows accumulation on one side only; without the southern losses it is consistent with sand being added to the shore overall.
whyWrong.C: The 1997 figures establish that the stations started similar. That is useful background, but it records no change and so supports no conclusion about the groyne.
whyWrong.D: One station's 7-metre loss shows erosion in the south but says nothing about the compensating gain in the north that makes it a redistribution.

commonMistakes: Citing only the side of the structure that changed most, when the claim is about a transfer and therefore needs both sides.

whyCorrect: The stated limit on line length is that the current weakens and eventually cannot move the instrument. A relay removes that limit: the weak arriving current only trips a switch, and a fresh local battery drives the next stretch. So the length is no longer set by the signal's decay but by how far you can keep installing relays and their batteries.

whyWrong.A: Direction is not what the passage is about. Nothing in the description of a relay restricts it to one-way working.
whyWrong.C: The whole point of a relay is that it works as an automatic switch; the text never suggests a person is needed at each one.
whyWrong.D: Adding relays and batteries at intervals adds cost per kilometre if anything, and the passage offers no cost comparison at all.

tips: An inference blank should follow from the stated obstacle and the stated fix — ask what limit has just been removed.

whyCorrect: Chain the facts: sulphides stay inert only while out of contact with air; mining exposes fresh sulphide surfaces and the pumping admits air to them; when the pumps stop, water rises through those same roadways and reaches the surface. Water passing over air-weathered sulphide picks up acid, so the discharge after closure should be more acid than anything the working mine produced.

whyWrong.B: Roof collapse is never mentioned, and the passage traces a chemical consequence, not a structural one.
whyWrong.C: Stopping the pumps lets water rise, so the water table goes up across the workings, not down.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the outcome the chain of facts points to; the rising water carries the products of weathered sulphide into surface streams.

commonMistakes: Skipping the detail that pumping admitted air, which is what makes the flooding after closure worse rather than harmless.

whyCorrect: What follows the blank is a list — gas, coke, tar, ammoniacal liquor — that spells out the "four things" already announced. A colon is the mark that introduces a list after a complete statement, and "A nineteenth-century gasworks sold four things from that one operation" is complete. So the colon is required.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must join two independent clauses. "Gas for lighting, coke for furnaces …" is a list of noun phrases with no verb, so it cannot stand as a clause.
whyWrong.B: "And" plus a comma would make the list an added element rather than the enumeration of the four things just promised, and it leaves the list itself dangling without an introducing mark.
whyWrong.C: Running "operation" straight into "gas" with no punctuation gives no boundary between the statement and the list it introduces.

tips: A complete sentence followed by a list of examples takes a colon.

whyCorrect: The sentence already opens a dash before "an undercut, a boss on the side of the casting, for instance." That parenthetical interrupts the subject ("Anything that would lock the pattern in place") from its verb ("has to be made"), and a dash used on one side must be closed with a matching dash. So the second dash is the only mark that completes the pair.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon cannot close a dash, and it would need an independent clause on each side; "has to be made as a separate piece of sand" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.B: A colon cannot close a dash either, and what follows is the sentence's own predicate, not a list or explanation being introduced.
whyWrong.D: A comma cannot close a dash. Mixing the two marks leaves the parenthesis unbalanced.

commonMistakes: Not looking back for the opening dash, and so treating the blank as a free choice of pause mark rather than a required closing partner.

whyCorrect: There are two complete sentences here: "a colony disturbed a few times over the winter may reach spring with nothing left" and "the same disturbance in summer costs the animals very little." "However" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot splice them. A semicolon before it and a comma after it is the standard punctuation.

whyWrong.A: A colon announces something that explains or specifies what precedes it; here the second clause contrasts with the first, and a colon is not used before a conjunctive adverb joining two clauses.
whyWrong.C: A comma before "however" produces a comma splice — two independent clauses joined by a comma, which a conjunctive adverb cannot repair.
whyWrong.D: This runs the two clauses together with no boundary mark at all, leaving a fused sentence.

tips: "However," "therefore" and "moreover" joining two independent clauses always need a semicolon (or a period) in front of them.

whyCorrect: "A single door propped open short-circuits the current and leaves a whole district without air" is a complete sentence, and "young boys were once employed for no other purpose …" is another. Two independent clauses with no coordinating conjunction between them require a semicolon or a period; the semicolon is the choice offered.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse, and "air young boys" momentarily reads as one noun phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by "and" is not a standard construction; the colon already does the joining work, so the conjunction is redundant and ungrammatical here.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Testing only whether the sentence sounds acceptable aloud instead of checking whether each side of the blank is an independent clause.

whyCorrect: "Of the two" fixes the number of things being compared at exactly two, and English uses the comparative — not the superlative — for a two-way comparison. "Short" is a one-syllable adjective, so its comparative is formed with the ending: shorter.

whyWrong.A: "Most" forms a superlative, which needs three or more items, and short takes endings rather than "more/most" anyway.
whyWrong.C: "Shortest" is the superlative; with only two alignments in play there is no third for one to be shortest of.
whyWrong.D: "More shorter" doubles the comparative. A word may take the ending or "more," never both.

tips: "Of the two" is a reliable signal that the comparative form is required.

whyCorrect: Unpack the relative clause: the night shift was given to the two operators. The relative pronoun is the object of the preposition "to," and the objective form of "who" is "whom." Since the operators are people, "whom" is the only fit.

whyWrong.B: "Which" refers to things, not people, and the antecedent here is the two operators.
whyWrong.C: "Whose" is possessive and would need a noun after it — "to whose desk," for example — but the next word is "the night shift," the subject of the clause's own verb.
whyWrong.D: "Who" is the subject form. Directly after the preposition "to" the pronoun is an object, so "who" cannot stand.

commonMistakes: Choosing "who" because it sounds more familiar; test it by rewriting the clause as a plain sentence — "the shift was given to them" shows an object is needed.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with a modifying phrase, "Surveyed from the surface every fortnight throughout the drive," and whatever that phrase describes has to be the subject of the main clause. What was surveyed is the two headings, so the main clause must start with them. "The two headings proved to be only fifty millimetres apart" puts the right noun in the right place.

whyWrong.A: "There" is a placeholder subject; it names nothing that could have been surveyed, so the modifier dangles.
whyWrong.B: This makes the engineers the thing surveyed from the surface, which is not what the phrase means — they did the surveying.
whyWrong.C: This makes "the meeting" the thing surveyed every fortnight, but the meeting happened once, at the end, and it was the headings that were tracked throughout.

tips: After an opening participial phrase, check the very first noun of the main clause — that noun must be what the phrase describes.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences give a cause: the skin has stopped shrinking while the core is still contracting, which sets up internal stress. The sentence after the blank names the consequence — the places where a quench crack turns up. The transition has to be causal, so "For this reason" fits.

whyWrong.A: "By contrast" would need the crack locations to oppose the cooling description; they follow from it instead.
whyWrong.B: "In other words" signals a restatement, but the sentence introduces new information about where cracks appear.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" signals that the result runs against expectation, whereas cracking at an abrupt change of section is exactly what uneven shrinkage predicts.

commonMistakes: Choosing a contrast word because the sentence introduces a new subject; the relationship, not the novelty, decides the transition.

whyCorrect: Before the blank the open pit looks cheap: big machines, a fraction of the underground cost per tonne. After the blank comes the offsetting burden — all the barren rock over the ore must be shifted too, and the waste ratio worsens with depth. That is a drawback set against an advantage, so a contrast transition is needed.

whyWrong.A: "Consequently" would make the waste-stripping a result of the low haulage cost, but the two are independent facts pulling in opposite directions.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" signals a second point of the same kind; the second half undercuts the first rather than echoing it.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would make the overburden an example of cheap haulage, which it is not — it is an added cost.

tips: Ask whether the second half helps or hurts the first half's claim; hurting means a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences describe a defence built to trap an attacker between three rising walls and a ditch, under fire from both sides. The sentence after the blank reports the outcome — a thousand years of successful defence. Outcome following from design calls for a result transition.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" would mean the city held out despite the walls, which reverses the relationship the passage builds.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would present the thousand-year record as one example of the walls' arrangement, but it is a consequence, not an illustration of the layout.
whyWrong.D: "By contrast" needs an opposition; the record of successful defence agrees with the description of the fortifications.

commonMistakes: Being pulled toward a contrast word by the clause about the city eventually falling, which is a later concession inside the same sentence, not the relationship the blank marks.

whyCorrect: The goal names a specific job: explain how the square changed what happens after a refrigerator failure. That requires the before (whole batches discarded on suspicion, because a spoiled dose looks like a sound one) and the after (the square shows which vials actually overheated, so the good ones are kept). Only this choice joins those notes into that comparison.

whyWrong.B: This is a single note copied out. It describes the device but says nothing about refrigerator failures or what changed.
whyWrong.C: This describes the routine of reading the indicator before a dose, which is not the same as what happens after a failure.
whyWrong.D: This gives the temperature limits — background to why the problem exists, with no mention of the square or of the change in practice.

tips: When the goal says "changed," the answer has to contain both the old practice and the new one.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why the shield worked where earlier attempts failed, and the notes give the failure mode: the river broke in. So the answer must connect the shield's design to that specific danger. This choice does it — the frame supported the face and brickwork followed immediately, so no open length of tunnel was ever exposed to the river.

whyWrong.A: The shipworm explains where Brunel got the idea, not why the method kept the river out.
whyWrong.B: An opening date records that the tunnel succeeded; it does not explain the reason for the success.
whyWrong.C: This describes the shield and its patent date but stops short of linking it to the flooding that defeated the earlier attempts.

commonMistakes: Selecting a true note about the shield instead of the one sentence that answers the "why" the goal asks for.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why grain size matters, so the answer needs a consequence that differs with grain size. The notes supply both halves: fine sand is carried offshore within a season or two, while one beach given coarser sand held its width for eleven years. Setting those against each other shows grain size determines how long the nourishment lasts.

whyWrong.A: This defines what a nourishment scheme is and never mentions grain size.
whyWrong.B: This is a limitation of nourishment generally — it does not address the cause of erosion — and it applies whatever the grain size.
whyWrong.C: This states that the imported sand may be coarser or finer, but stops before saying what difference that makes.

tips: A "why does X matter" goal is answered by a note pair showing different outcomes for different values of X.

whyCorrect: The measuring stick is given in the sentence itself: "judged against the coal actually present." Up to half the coal in a panel stays locked in the pillars, and it can only be recovered by letting the roof collapse. Measured against what is there, leaving half of it underground is wasteful.

whyWrong.B: The pillars do protect the roof, but the sentence asks how the method rates against the coal available, not what it does for safety.
whyWrong.C: "Exhaustive" would mean the method takes everything out, which is the opposite of leaving half the seam standing.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the passage suggests the yield varies unpredictably; the loss is a known, built-in feature of the layout.

commonMistakes: Answering with what the pillars are for instead of with the judgement the stated criterion forces.

whyCorrect: The described system throws away all but a few hundred of tens of millions of collisions, and only the survivors reach disk. The decision the designers make in advance is which events are worth retaining, so the physics that can be reported later is bounded by that choice. "Keeping" names the selection the passage describes.

whyWrong.B: Every event is examined for coarse features — measurement of a sort happens to all of them. The limiting step is what is saved afterwards.
whyWrong.C: Funding is never mentioned; the constraint described is a recording bottleneck, not a financial one.
whyWrong.D: Publication happens long after, on data already on disk. It cannot be the thing decided "in advance" that limits what data exist.

tips: Match the blank to the specific action the passage's mechanism performs, not to a plausible-sounding activity in the same field.

whyCorrect: The contrast in the passage is between a machine that cuts and lines at the same moment and drill-and-blast, which leaves rock bare until a lining crew arrives later. The advantage being named is that excavation and support happen together rather than in sequence, which is simultaneity.

whyWrong.A: Novelty is never at issue; the machine's benefit is described in terms of timing, not of being new.
whyWrong.C: "Separation" describes the drill-and-blast case the passage treats as inferior, so it reverses the point.
whyWrong.D: Cost is never mentioned, and expense would be a drawback rather than the advantage the sentence is naming.

commonMistakes: Reading "not speed alone" as "not speed at all" and then looking for an unrelated virtue instead of the timing relationship just described.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets "resolve two echoes" against a long call that "runs them together." The bat's problem is telling the moth's echo apart from the leaves' echo when the two arrive a fraction of a millisecond apart. So "resolve" here means to separate them perceptually — to distinguish them as two.

whyWrong.A: This is the everyday sense of resolving to do something. A call cannot make a decision, and no course of action is in view.
whyWrong.C: Breaking a thing into simpler parts is analysis; here two already-distinct echoes need to be told apart, not decomposed.
whyWrong.D: Settling a dispute is another familiar sense, but there are no parties in conflict in this passage.

tips: With a familiar word underlined, the test is almost always a less common sense — use the contrast term ("runs together") to pin the meaning.

whyCorrect: The passage's point is that a groyne does not create sand, it intercepts it, so the pile on the updrift side comes at the expense of beaches beyond the last groyne. A verdict based on one spot would miss the loss elsewhere, so the works have to be judged across the whole length of coast they affect.

whyWrong.A: Sand height at the groyne is exactly the local measure the passage warns against, since that sand was taken from somewhere else.
whyWrong.B: No seasonal difference is mentioned anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: Timber cost is never raised; the argument is about where the sand goes, not what the structure costs.

commonMistakes: Picking the measure the passage names first, when the second half of the passage exists to say that measure is incomplete.

whyCorrect: The text moves through two linked things. First a change in how the army was maintained: coin from taxation gives way to soldiers settled on land who draw their living from it. Then the effect on provincial administration: districts named after the units in them, and commanders holding civil as well as military authority. The purpose covers both.

whyWrong.B: No comparison of effectiveness is offered. The passage explains a change in support, not which arrangement fought better.
whyWrong.C: Taxation appears only as the earlier source of pay; how taxes were assessed is never described.
whyWrong.D: No individual commander is named or followed; commanders are mentioned only as a class whose powers widened.

tips: A main-purpose choice must account for the last sentence too, not just the first half of the passage.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences lay out a framework — the coast as a closed compartment with sand entering, travelling and leaving, so a loss in one place is a gain in another. The last sentence takes that framework and runs one case through it: armouring a cliff saves the houses but starves the beaches downdrift. Framework, then application.

whyWrong.A: No history is given. There are no dates, projects or sequence of developments in the text.
whyWrong.B: The passage relies on sand travelling along the coast; it never disputes that it does.
whyWrong.D: Only one intervention is discussed, and no recommendation between alternatives is made.

commonMistakes: Treating the cliff-armouring sentence as the topic when it is the illustration of the model set up before it.

whyCorrect: Every detail builds one picture: workers filled until they cannot walk, hanging in a chamber for months, dispensing a drop of liquid when forage fails. The closing sentence spells it out — a run of good weeks turned into a store safe from drying and from theft. These ants function as living storage vessels for a surplus.

whyWrong.A: Colony size is never compared across regions.
whyWrong.C: The passage says forage sometimes fails but never attributes that to heat or describes when the ants forage.
whyWrong.D: The immobile ants stay in the nest and are fed and tapped there; nothing says they are removed.

tips: When the last sentence generalises, check your choice against it — that sentence usually states the main idea outright.

whyCorrect: The passage gives the mechanism in one clause: a reagent clings to the mineral surface and makes it repel water, and air blown through the pulp lifts those water-repelling particles into a froth. The rock, still wetted, sinks. So the rise comes from a surface property plus attachment to bubbles.

whyWrong.B: Nothing dissolves. The mineral stays a solid particle and rides up on bubbles.
whyWrong.C: The stirring disperses the crushed ore into the water; it is the air and the reagent, not agitation, that sort mineral from rock.
whyWrong.D: Density is not the basis of the separation; the passage says the difference exploited is one of wetting.

commonMistakes: Assuming a flotation process must work on density, when the text explicitly names surface wetting as the difference.

whyCorrect: The claim is that the tag attached to the hero is picked for the metrical space it fills, not for what it says about him at that moment. This quotation attaches "Marko of the sharp sword" to him twice in one breath, while he is sleeping and then calling for wine — moments in which a sword is irrelevant. The phrase is doing structural work, not descriptive work, which is exactly what the scholar argues.

whyWrong.A: This describes the performance setting. It contains no descriptive tag for the hero at all.
whyWrong.B: This is a narrative event involving his mother; no recurring epithet appears, so it cannot show how epithets are used.
whyWrong.D: Here the sharp sword is drawn and does the work of the sentence, so the phrase fits the moment — the opposite of the scholar's point.

tips: To illustrate a claim about a formula, look for the phrase repeating where it does not fit, not where it does.

whyCorrect: Vandersteen's argument has two parts: no worker is directed, and thresholds differ between individuals. This finding matches both — repair need rises, unassigned nurses take it up on their own, and the ones who switch first are those least readily triggered to nurse, which is what differing thresholds predicts. Nothing about it requires an instruction to be issued.

whyWrong.A: An age difference between foragers and nurses is compatible with a fixed schedule of roles and says nothing about local cues or individual thresholds.
whyWrong.B: The queen's egg-laying concerns reproduction, not how workers allocate themselves to tasks.
whyWrong.D: Faster repair in larger colonies is explained by having more workers available; it does not distinguish self-organisation from central direction.

commonMistakes: Choosing a finding that is merely consistent with the argument instead of one that tests the specific mechanism it proposes.

whyCorrect: The critic says the novel treats the clerk's work as imagination rather than calculation. In this quotation the clerk has to picture the ship, her master and the March ice — "the whole of a voyage that had not yet happened" — before he can set a rate. That is the imaginative act the critic describes, stated in the clerk's own words.

whyWrong.B: A rate quoted from eleven years of office custom is the opposite of imagination; it is precedent applied mechanically.
whyWrong.C: This is routine and office furniture — hours and ruled ledgers — with no account of how the work is done.
whyWrong.D: The chief's remark makes arithmetic the requirement, which supports calculation rather than imagination.

tips: For "which quotation illustrates," the quotation must show the claimed quality happening, not merely mention the same subject.

whyCorrect: The passage sets the condition for spread as each case producing more than one further case, and then says a disease that spreads readily needs a larger immune fraction than one that spreads with difficulty. The variable doing the work in that comparison is how readily the disease spreads, so the required vaccination proportion is fixed by its contagiousness.

whyWrong.A: Immunity elsewhere does not shrink this population's susceptible pool; the argument is about the fraction immune within the population in question.
whyWrong.B: Duration of immunity would affect how often vaccination must be repeated, but the passage never raises it and it is not what the comparison turns on.
whyWrong.D: Severity affects how much you care about preventing the disease, not the threshold at which the chain of transmission dies out.

commonMistakes: Substituting how dangerous a disease is for how transmissible it is; only transmissibility appears in the passage's chain of reasoning.

whyCorrect: The scheme described requires changing voltage three times, and the only device offered for that is the transformer. The passage states the catch: a transformer "will do nothing at all with a steady current." So the supply must be one whose current keeps reversing — alternating current — or no voltage change is possible.

whyWrong.A: Insulation material is never mentioned and does not address the transformer's requirement.
whyWrong.C: Large conductors would cut resistance losses directly, which is the alternative the passage sets aside in favour of raising voltage.
whyWrong.D: Short distances would avoid the loss problem entirely, but the passage is explaining how long-distance transmission was made to work, not how it was avoided.

tips: When a passage names a device and then names its one limitation, the blank almost always states what that limitation demands.

whyCorrect: Strip the sentence to its bones: the subject is "A loss deliberately incurred to save the whole venture" and the verb is "is borne." No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb, so the blank takes nothing at all.

whyWrong.A: A comma here cuts the subject off from its own verb, which Standard English does not allow.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides; "is borne by every interest in it" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.C: A colon also requires a complete statement before it, and "A loss deliberately incurred to save the whole venture" is only a noun phrase.

commonMistakes: Inserting a comma because the subject is long. Length does not license the break; only structure does.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand alone: "The commissioners cut the excerpts to a fiftieth of their original length" and "they gave the result the force of law and forbade any commentary on it." Two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction "and" take a comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses on its own; adding "and" as well doubles the join.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation, list or specification, and it is not paired with a coordinating conjunction.
whyWrong.D: Dropping the comma before "and" between two full clauses leaves the boundary unmarked, and "length and they gave" reads as a compound object at first.

tips: Independent clause + comma + FANBOYS + independent clause is the pattern to check for here.

whyCorrect: The first part is a complete sentence ending on "the one thing that keeps it in existence," and what follows names that one thing: the feet of ants still finding food there. A colon is the mark that introduces an identification after a complete statement, which is precisely this construction.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "in existence the feet of ants" runs the noun phrase into the sentence with nothing to show it is the promised identification.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, but "the feet of ants that are still finding food at the end of it" is a noun phrase with no main verb.
whyWrong.D: "And the feet of ants…" would make the noun phrase a second item joined to the first clause, which leaves it grammatically stranded — there is no verb for it.

tips: When a sentence promises "the one thing" and then names it, the mark between them is a colon.

whyCorrect: "Although" makes everything up to "can be made" a subordinate clause, and the main clause is "physicists worked through millions of such photographs." A subordinate clause placed in front of its main clause is separated from it by a comma.

whyWrong.A: A colon must follow a complete statement, but an "Although" clause is dependent and cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: "And" would try to coordinate a dependent clause with an independent one, which produces a sentence with no main clause for "Although" to attach to.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon also needs independent clauses on both sides, and the "Although" clause is not one.

commonMistakes: Treating a long opening clause as a sentence in its own right; the subordinating word at the front is what makes it dependent.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The underwriters on the slip." A phrase beginning "together with" is parenthetical and never changes the number of the subject, so the broker does not make it singular or add to it grammatically. A plural subject takes the plural verb "receive."

whyWrong.B: "Has received" is singular and also shifts to the perfect, which clashes with the habitual "as soon as it is issued."
whyWrong.C: "Receives" is the singular form, agreeing with "broker" instead of with the real subject, "underwriters."
whyWrong.D: "Is receiving" is singular and progressive; the sentence states a standing practice, not something in progress.

tips: Phrases like "together with," "as well as" and "along with" are invisible to subject-verb agreement — cross them out before choosing the verb.

whyCorrect: "Since the aluminium works opened" marks a period that begins in the past and runs up to now, and "in every year but one" covers all of that span. English uses the present perfect for a stretch of time reaching the present, so "has risen" is right.

whyWrong.A: The past perfect places an event before some other past point, and no earlier past reference point is given here.
whyWrong.B: The simple present "rises" states a general habit and cannot cover a completed count of years since a stated starting event.
whyWrong.C: The simple past "rose" would close the period off in the past, but "since" keeps it open to the present.

commonMistakes: Matching the tense to "opened" rather than to the time frame "since" creates.

whyCorrect: "A number of" is a plural quantifier — it means several — and takes a plural verb, unlike "the number of," which is singular. The counters, plural, were changed during a completed past event, the shutdown last winter, so the simple past plural "were" is correct.

whyWrong.A: "Was" is singular and does not agree with the plural sense of "a number of the counters."
whyWrong.C: "Has been" is singular and in the present perfect, which conflicts with the finished, dated time "last winter."
whyWrong.D: "Is" is singular and present tense; the change happened last winter.

tips: "A number of" takes a plural verb; "the number of" takes a singular one.

whyCorrect: The passage builds a chain: uniform pricing draws in the worst risks, the healthy stay out, so the remaining pool is worse than the price assumed. The next step — the price has to rise — follows directly from that deterioration. A result transition is what the blank needs.

whyWrong.A: "By contrast" would set the price rise against what precedes it, but the price rise is caused by what precedes it.
whyWrong.B: "For example" would make the price rise an instance of the worsening pool rather than its consequence.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" signals something happening in spite of the previous point; a rise is exactly what a worse-than-priced pool forces.

tips: Follow the causal chain sentence by sentence — if each step forces the next, the transition is a result word.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the machine's strength — it drives a bore faster than any other method. The sentence after the blank gives the offsetting weakness: unexpected ground stops it for months. That is a concession running against the advantage just stated, so "Even so" fits.

whyWrong.B: "In other words" would mean the second sentence restates the first, but it introduces a drawback the first sentence did not contain.
whyWrong.C: "For example" would make the months-long hold-up an illustration of the machine's speed, which it contradicts.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" claims the two sentences point the same way; they point in opposite directions.

commonMistakes: Reading the first sentence's mention of a particular diameter and ground as neutral setup, when it is the setup for the failure case.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a benefit of adding material: more interactions, so more sensitivity. The second gives the price of the same action: extra scattering, so worse direction measurement. Benefit against cost is a contrast, and "However" marks it.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" signals a parallel point, but the second sentence undercuts rather than echoes the first.
whyWrong.B: "For this reason" would make the scattering a consequence pursued because of the sensitivity gain, when it is an unwanted side effect.
whyWrong.D: "In fact" strengthens or confirms the previous claim; here the second sentence qualifies it.

tips: A sentence containing "also" plus a drawback almost always follows a contrast transition, not an additive one.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how the tradition can be fixed and variable at once, so the answer must hold both properties together and say where each lives. This choice puts the variability in the length of performances and the fixity in the praise-names, genealogies and proverbs recurring word for word — the material is fixed, the whole is not.

whyWrong.A: This tells you who performs the epic and how they train. It addresses neither fixity nor variation.
whyWrong.B: Printed versions freezing one performance is a consequence of publication, not an account of how the oral tradition itself is both stable and changing.
whyWrong.D: How performers describe their role is a claim about self-understanding; it does not identify what stays constant and what varies.

tips: When a goal names two apparently opposed properties, the answer has to locate each one in a different part of the evidence.

whyCorrect: The goal is to say what pumped storage does for the grid despite its losses, so the answer must contain both the benefit and the acknowledged cost. This choice gives the reason it is needed (large plant cannot start and stop quickly), the service it provides (cheap overnight energy returned within a minute at the peak), and the price paid (a quarter of the energy).

whyWrong.A: This is only the cost. Given alone it makes the station look like a pure loss and never says what it accomplishes.
whyWrong.C: This describes the demand pattern, which is the background problem, not what the station does about it.
whyWrong.D: This gives half the cycle — the pumping — with no mention of the fast release that makes it useful, and no mention of the losses.

commonMistakes: Choosing a single true note when the goal's "despite" wording requires two facts set against each other.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why the courts acted against a method that worked well, so the answer has to connect the method's effectiveness to the harm it caused. This choice does both: the nozzle's enormous output is exactly what sent gravel downstream, raising riverbeds until towns that had never flooded were flooding in ordinary winters — the damage that would prompt a court to act.

whyWrong.B: This records the ruling itself. It states the outcome the question asks you to explain, not the reason for it.
whyWrong.C: This shows only that the method worked well, which is the half of the question already granted.
whyWrong.D: This defines hydraulic mining without mentioning any consequence downstream.

tips: A "why did X happen" goal needs the causal link, and a note that simply reports X happening is never the answer.
